tour.itineraries:
Day 1 — Arrival and Orientation Cycling in Luang Prabang
Meet the guide and team upon arrival in Luang Prabang. A short sunset ride around the town provides acclimatization and a gauge of fitness levels before the journey begins. An informal briefing and dinner follow at Khaiphaen Restaurant, a vocational training establishment. Overnight in Luang Prabang.

Day 2 — Kuang Si Waterfalls and Trek to Ban Long Lao Mai
Depart early by bicycle on the mountain road leading south from Luang Prabang to Kuang Si Waterfalls, approximately 30 kilometers on tarmac. The falls feature turquoise pools suitable for swimming. After lunch—Laos-style grilled meat and vegetables—leave bicycles behind and trek through forest to Ban Long Lao Mai, a village where Khmu families and Hmong residents, resettled by the government following the end of Laos's civil war, now live. The two communities historically occupied distinct territories; integration occurred gradually over decades. Dinner is shared with a homestay family. Overnight in Ban Long Lao Mai.

Day 3 — Jungle Trek from Ban Long Lao Mai to Nong Khouay
Breakfast with the homestay family begins the day. A 9-kilometer trek through the valley over approximately 3 hours brings you to Nong Khouay, a village without grid electricity or mobile signal. The small central shop serves as a gathering point. Villagers are accustomed to visitors and offer conversation over coffee or beer. In the evening, a village elder may share local history and observations. Overnight in Nong Khouay.

Day 4 — Cycling the Nam Ou Valley to Nong Khiaw
A one-hour descent on dirt road leads to the start of the northbound cycling route. The route skirts the Nam Ou River valley, passing Pak Mong village where lunch occurs, before entering an area of tall limestone karst formations. The landscape shifts noticeably as the valley narrows and elevation rises. Terrain includes dirt and tarmac sections. Total distance is approximately 80 kilometers. Overnight in Nong Khiaw.

Day 5 — Nam Ou River Boat Journey to Muang Khua
A 4–5 hour boat ride travels upriver through the Nam Ou gorge to Muang Khua. The river route passes primary forest on both banks and includes stops at remote villages accessible only by water. Overnight in Muang Khua.

Day 6 — Cycling Through Primary Forest to the Laos–Vietnam Border and Dien Bien Phu
A 60-kilometer cycling day crosses from Laos into Vietnam. Much of the route runs through primary forest; the road surface combines tarmac and unpaved sections. The route passes through villages of hill-tribe communities. At the border, a Vietnamese guide takes over transport to Dien Bien Phu, located in the Muong Thanh Valley. The city is known internationally as the site of a battle that marked the end of French colonial rule in Indochina. The valley is also known for wet rice cultivation and Tai ethnic dance traditions. Overnight in Dien Bien Phu.

Day 7 — Cycling Through Tai Communities to Tuan Giao
An 80-kilometer cycle through villages populated primarily by Tai ethnic groups leads to Tuan Giao. One significant climb occurs at a mountain pass approximately 15 kilometers outside Dien Bien Phu. Overall terrain is considered moderate. Overnight in a guesthouse in Tuan Giao.

Day 8 — Pha Din Pass Descent and Cycling to Son La
A short vehicle transfer ascends to Pha Din Pass (known locally as the "Heaven and Earth" pass), situated at approximately 1,450 meters. From the summit, a 15-kilometer downhill section descends through green rice fields and karst valleys with minimal traffic. The descent passes through areas where Tai and Hmong communities live, with agricultural activity visible throughout. Total cycling distance from the pass to Son La is significant. Overnight in a hotel in Son La.

Day 9 — Gradual Descent Through Rice Terraces to Moc Chau
A short vehicle transfer precedes a 45-kilometer cycling day with gentle downhill gradient. The route runs beneath limestone cliffs and through terraced rice paddies. Afternoon cycling passes through agricultural landscapes dominated by rice cultivation. Overnight in Moc Chau.

Day 10 — Black Tai Communities and Tea Plantations to Mai Chau
A 45-kilometer cycling day on quiet back roads enters territory primarily inhabited by Black Tai (Tai Dam) communities. As elevation rises to approximately 1,000 meters near Mai Chau, the landscape transitions to include plum orchards, corn fields, and tea plantations. Road surfaces are narrow and receive light traffic. Overnight in a homestay in Mai Chau.

Day 11 — Ma River Valley Cycling and Transfer to Cuc Phuong National Park
An 80-kilometer cycling day follows the Ma River through working agricultural land where subsistence farming and crop cultivation remain visible throughout. In late afternoon, a vehicle transfer takes you to Cuc Phuong National Park, Vietnam's important nature reserve containing the country's largest area of primary forest. A visit to the Primate Rescue Centre provides information on species recovery efforts, including the Cat Ba Langur, one of the world's most endangered primates. Overnight in a park bungalow.

Day 12 — Final Cycling Through Cuc Phuong Forest to Hanoi
A final 40-kilometer cycling section traverses Cuc Phuong forest to the park center. After a tea break, a vehicle transfer completes the journey to Hanoi. Guide and driver support is available for the final leg. End of services.

output.subtitle: A 12-day cycling and boat journey from Luang Prabang through the Nam Ou gorge, across the Laos-Vietnam border, and down to Hanoi via Pha Din Pass and Cuc Phuong National Park
output.summary:
This 12-day route is built for families with older children and teenagers who cycle regularly and want a journey that asks something of them. Starting in Luang Prabang, the route heads north along the Nam Ou River valley, passes through Khmu and Hmong villages, and crosses into northern Vietnam. From there, it descends through Dien Bien Phu, over the Pha Din Pass at 1,450 meters, through Black Tai communities in the Mai Chau valley, and into Cuc Phuong National Park before finishing in Hanoi.

Daily cycling ranges from 40 to 80 kilometers across tarmac, unpaved mountain tracks, and riverside roads. The itinerary also includes a 4-5 hour river boat journey through the Nam Ou gorge, two days of forest trekking, and vehicle transfers where terrain makes them the right call. Accommodation moves between hotels, guesthouses, and family homestays, including two nights in villages without grid electricity. Parents should read this as genuinely active travel with basic conditions on some nights, suited to teenagers and confident younger cyclists aged around 12 and up.

What carries the route beyond the physical effort is what families encounter along the way: highland communities with distinct histories, a valley that shaped the end of colonial rule in Indochina, primary forest that is still home to some of the world's most endangered primates, and villages where daily life looks nothing like home. The learning here is not scripted; it happens in conversation, over shared meals, and on roads that pass through living landscapes.

tour.name: Mongolia: Khövsgöl Lake and Gobi Desert — 15 Days
tour.subtitle: From the Siberian Taiga forests of Khövsgöl Lake to the Gobi's Flaming Cliffs and sand dunes, crossing Mongolia's northern steppes and central plateaus.
tour.summary: This 15-day itinerary traces a north-to-south arc through Mongolia's distinct ecosystems and historical centers. The route begins at Khövsgöl Lake, Asia's second-largest freshwater lake and home to the Tsaatan reindeer herders, then moves through volcanic regions and ancient monastic sites before descending into the Gobi Desert. The journey encounters dormant volcanoes, paleontological landmarks, granite rock formations, and the layered ruins of centers that shaped Mongolian culture—from the 13th-century capital Kharkhorin to the now-silent monastic complexes of Amarbayasgalant, Erdene Zuu, and Ongi. Overnight accommodation is in standard ger camps positioned near each region's key sites; all meals and ground transportation between stages are included.

tour.itineraries:
Day 1 — Arrival in Ulaanbaatar
Arrive at Chinggis Khaan International Airport. The local team meets you for transfer to the city center, where you check into your hotel and gather for a welcome dinner.

Day 2 — Amarbayasgalant Monastery and the Road to Darkhan
Depart for Darkhan, one of Mongolia's two largest cities outside Ulaanbaatar, approximately 350 kilometers north. After lunch in Darkhan, continue toward Amarbayasgalant Monastery, reaching it in the late afternoon. Built in 1727 using traditional woodworking techniques, the monastery stands as one of the three major monastic centers in the country. Unlike most Mongolian monasteries damaged during the political purges of the 1930s, Amarbayasgalant survived in relatively intact condition—its construction contains no metal beams or nails. The surrounding monastic grounds and nearby hills offer meditative walking experiences. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 3 — Uran Togoo Volcano and Nomadic Family Visit
Journey to Uran Togoo, a dormant volcano that erupted approximately 24,000 years ago. The volcano sits within green steppes and forests, the largest of four dormant volcanoes in the surrounding valleys. The crater measures 600 meters wide and 50–60 meters deep, descending into a walkable caldera. The area offers trekking opportunities across volcanic terrain. After lunch in the town of Bulgan, visit a local nomadic family to observe traditional herding practices that have persisted and adapted into the modern era. Arrive at Sod Camp in the afternoon. The camp sits opposite a mountain range with trekking access and proximity to a mineral spring with reputed healing properties. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 4 — Khövsgöl Lake: Journey to Mongolia's Second-Largest Freshwater Lake
Travel approximately 350 kilometers northward to reach Lake Khövsgöl, the tour's primary destination. Stop for lunch near Moron, capital of Khövsgöl province, before continuing to the lakeshore camp. Khövsgöl spans 2,760 square kilometers and formed approximately two million years ago. The lake sits at the boundary between Central Asian steppes and Siberian Taiga forests, creating a distinct ecological zone. It is home to the Tsaatan people, also known as the Dukha, who sustain themselves primarily through reindeer herding and represent one of the country's most unique ethnic groups. Overnight in a standard ger camp (upgrade available).

Day 5 — Khövsgöl Lake: Optional Activities
A free day at the lake. Optional activities include boat rides on the water, horseback riding across surrounding terrain, visits to local nomadic families, excursions to Tsaatan reindeer herders' settlements, and trekking along shorelines and forest paths. Overnight in a standard ger camp (upgrades available).

Day 6 — Ulziit Khishig Camp
Depart in the morning toward Ulziit Khishig Camp, positioned 210 kilometers south along the route toward the tour's next destinations. The camp sits in a verdant valley surrounded by hillside forests. Overnight in a standard ger camp (cabin upgrade available).

Day 7 — Khorgo-Terkhiin Nuur National Park and Volcanic Crater Walk
Travel to Arkhangai province and Khorgo-Terkhiin Tsagaan Nuur National Park. The area centers on two landmarks: Terkhiin Tsagaan Lake, covering 61 square kilometers and home to numerous bird species, and the nearby dormant Khorgo volcano. The volcano erupted over 8,000 years ago; that eruption directly shaped the surrounding landscape and affected the formation of Terkhiin Tsagaan Lake. Visit the lake shores and trek to the volcano's crater rim for a panoramic view of the surrounding terrain. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 8 — Kharkhorin: Ancient Capital and Erdene Zuu Monastery
Drive toward Kharkhorin, located within the Orkhon Valley Cultural Landscape—a region where the history of Mongolia and the larger world took shape. Kharkhorin served as the capital of the Mongol Empire; the Kharkhorin Museum houses artifacts tracing origins to the Mongol dynasties and periods preceding them. The primary site visited is Erdene Zuu Monastery, the oldest Buddhist monastery in Mongolia, founded in the late 16th century. For centuries, thousands of monks inhabited this complex and shaped Mongolian cultural and artistic development. Political purges in the 1930s diminished its collections, but the monastic grounds were preserved. Both original temples and currently active temples remain accessible for visitation. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 9 — Ongi Monastery Ruins and Trek
Drive to the ruins of Ongi Monastery in Middle Gobi province, approximately 270 kilometers southeast. The monastery once stood on both banks of the Ongi River, from which it took its name. It ranks among the three major monastic centers in Mongolian history; at its peak, over 2,000 monks lived within its walls and shaped modern Mongolian art and culture. After lunch at the camp, trek the monastic grounds—currently undergoing gradual restoration—while learning its historical significance. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 10 — Bayanzag (Flaming Cliffs): Paleontology and Silk Road History
Drive approximately 190 kilometers to Bayanzag, known as the Flaming Cliffs for the fiery colors the rock face displays at sunset. The site holds significance both paleontologically and historically: it lies on the ancient Silk Road trade route and is where the world's first fossilized dinosaur eggs were discovered. After checking into camp and lunch, visit the local information center to learn about Roy Chapman Andrews's expeditions to the region—expeditions that inspired the character of Indiana Jones. The afternoon offers extensive trekking and photography opportunities across the Flaming Cliffs. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 11 — Khongor Sand Dunes: Singing Sand and Camel Trek
Drive approximately 170 kilometers to reach the Khongor Sand Dunes camp. After lunch and rest, visit a local nomadic family in the late afternoon and ride their camels to the dunes. The dunes are known locally as Singing Sand due to the distinctive sounds the sands produce during strong winds and avalanches. The dunes extend 120 kilometers in length and 6–12 kilometers in width. Trekking to the dune tops provides expansive views of the surrounding landscape. The Khongor River flows nearby, its water supporting local greenery and life. Overnight in a standard ger camp (upgrade available).

Day 12 — Yol Valley and Gurvan Saikhan National Park: Vultures and Wildlife
Travel approximately 220 kilometers toward Gurvan Saikhan National Park. Check into camp and have lunch, then depart for Yol Valley, nicknamed Vulture Valley for the bearded vultures that nest on the tall cliffs rising above 2,000 meters. The valley lies within Gurvan Saikhan National Park, home to Argali wild sheep, Ibex, snow leopards, and falcons; sightings depend on timing and luck. Yol Valley is also known for ice glaciers that form in winter and typically melt by early July. Trek through the valley with ample photography opportunities. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 13 — Tsagaan Suvarga (White Stupa): Colored Cliffs and Photography
Depart toward Middle Gobi to visit Tsagaan Suvarga—literally meaning White Stupa—named for the appearance of the local cliffs from a distance. Stop briefly in Mandalgobi for lunch. Upon arrival, check into the local camp and enjoy a relaxed afternoon. The cliffs can be visited in the late afternoon and again the following morning. The local soil composition creates varied natural colors across the rock face, making the site a notable destination for photography. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 14 — Baga Gazarin Chuluu: Granite Formations and Monastery Ruins
Depart toward Baga Gazarin Chuluu, a plateau characterized by exotic granite rock formations. After checking into the local ger camp and lunch, visit the ruins of an ancient monastery destroyed during the political purges of 1937. Walk among the rock formations themselves; the area offers trekking opportunities across distinctive terrain. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 15 — Return to Ulaanbaatar
220-kilometer drive.

Approximately 170 kilometers of driving reach the Khongor Sand Dunes camp. After lunch and rest, a visit to a local nomadic family in the late afternoon leads to a camel ride out to the dunes themselves — one of the most social, tactile moments on the whole route. The hiking here is straightforward and rewards a slow pace, with frequent stops for photography along the trail. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 13 — Tsagaan Suvarga: Colored Cliffs in Middle Gobi
The drive heads into Middle Gobi with a lunch stop in Mandalgobi before reaching Tsagaan Suvarga — White Stupa — named for the appearance of the cliffs from a distance. The varied soil composition produces a range of natural colors across the rock face, and the site works well in the late afternoon light. There is time to visit the cliffs on arrival and again the following morning before departure. A relaxed overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 14 — Baga Gazarin Chuluu: Granite Formations and 1937 Monastery Ruins
The final active day reaches Baga Gazarin Chuluu, a plateau of granite rock formations rising from the steppe. After checking into the local ger camp and lunch, the afternoon covers the ruins of a monastery destroyed in the political purges of 1937 and the rock formations themselves, which offer solid trekking across unusual terrain. A fitting last night in the Mongolian steppe before the drive back to Ulaanbaatar. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 1 · Arrival in Delhi
A private transfer from Delhi airport delivers you to your hotel, where the evening is yours to settle in at your own pace.

Day 2 · Delhi: Red Fort, Jama Masjid, Humayun's Tomb & Qutub Minar
A full day in the capital, guided through centuries of Islamic architecture. Your guide brings context to each monument: the Mughal ceremonial weight of the Red Fort, the vast congregational space of Jama Masjid, the garden geometry of Humayun's Tomb, and the composed solemnity of Qutub Minar. India Gate and the President's House frame the colonial-era city in between. Overnight in Delhi.

Day 3 · Delhi to Agra: Taj Mahal, Fort & Tombs
Transfer south to Agra. Visit the Taj Mahal, Agra Fort, Itmad-ud-Daulah, and Sikandra. Overnight in Agra.

Day 4 · Agra to Jaipur via Fatehpur Sikri
The drive west to Jaipur, approximately 235 km, pauses at Fatehpur Sikri, the sandstone capital Akbar raised and then quietly abandoned in the late 16th century. Its empty courts and audience halls give the guide room to explore why great Mughal ambitions sometimes outran the land itself. The evening is at leisure on arrival in Jaipur.

Day 5 · Jaipur: Amber Fort, Hawa Mahal & City Palace
A full day exploring Jaipur's architectural landmarks: Amber Fort's Rajput grandeur, the Hawa Mahal's iconic window screen, Jantar Mantar's astronomical instruments, and City Palace's blend of tradition and modernity. Overnight in Jaipur.

Day 6 · Jaipur to Khejarla via Pushkar
The route west, approximately 270 km, passes through Pushkar, a sacred lake town of considerable pilgrimage significance. Overnight at Khejarla.

Day 7 · Khejarla to Jodhpur: Mehrangarh Fort & Sadar Market
An 85 km drive to Jodhpur, where Mehrangarh Fort commands the skyline with a scale that rewards close attention. Your guide takes you through its ramparts and palace chambers, unpacking the Rathore dynasty's long hold on the Marwar region. Jaswant Thada's white marble cenotaph offers a quieter counterpoint before you continue to Umaid Bhawan Palace and the Clock Tower above Sadar Market. Overnight in Jodhpur.

Day 8 · Jodhpur to Udaipur via Ranakpur Jain Temples
The drive south passes through the Ranakpur Jain temple complex in the Aravalli hills, with its 15th-century main temple adorned with carved marble pillars. Evening at leisure by Udaipur's lakes and Jag Mandir. Overnight in Udaipur.

Day 9 · Udaipur: City Palace, Jagdish Temple & the Lakes
Udaipur rewards unhurried attention. The City Palace on its lakeside terrace holds centuries of Mewar history within its courtyards; the 17th-century Jagdish Temple stands just outside its gates with its own devotional atmosphere. Pichola and Fateh Sagar Lakes, the Crystal Gallery, and Gangaur Ghat round out a day that moves at a considered pace. Overnight in Udaipur.

Day 10 · Udaipur Morning, then Flight to Delhi
A relaxed morning in Udaipur before flying north to Delhi. Transfer to the hotel; the evening is at leisure.

Day 11 · Delhi to Khajuraho: Western Group Temples
A flight to Khajuraho opens one of India's most distinctive temple ensembles. Your guide leads you through the Western Group, where 11th-century sandstone temples carry carvings of remarkable iconographic depth, their figures drawn from devotional, courtly, and cosmological traditions. The evening light and sound show at the temple complex sets the monuments in narrative context. Overnight in Khajuraho.

Day 12 · Varanasi: Ganges Ghats and the Dashashwamedh Aarti
A flight to Varanasi, then an evening at the Ganges ghats, where Dashashwamedh Ghat's Aarti ceremony draws the day to a resonant close. Overnight in Varanasi.

Day 13 · Sarnath's Deer Park and Varanasi's Temples
Sarnath, a short distance from Varanasi, is where the Buddha delivered his first teaching; the deer park and museum hold sculpture and relics that your guide places within the wider arc of Buddhist history. The afternoon turns to Varanasi's temples. Overnight in Varanasi.

Day 14 · Varanasi to Delhi
A morning flight returns you to Delhi. Transfer to the hotel; the evening is yours.

Day 15 · Departure from Delhi
A private transfer to Delhi airport after breakfast for your onward journey.

tour.name: Mongolia: Khövsgöl Lake and Gobi Desert — 15 Days
tour.subtitle: From the Siberian Taiga forests of Khövsgöl Lake to the Gobi's Flaming Cliffs and sand dunes, crossing Mongolia's northern steppes and central plateaus.
tour.summary: This 15-day itinerary traces a north-to-south arc through Mongolia's distinct ecosystems and historical centers. The route begins at Khövsgöl Lake, Asia's second-largest freshwater lake and home to the Tsaatan reindeer herders, then moves through volcanic regions and ancient monastic sites before descending into the Gobi Desert. The journey encounters dormant volcanoes, paleontological landmarks, granite rock formations, and the layered ruins of centers that shaped Mongolian culture—from the 13th-century capital Kharkhorin to the now-silent monastic complexes of Amarbayasgalant, Erdene Zuu, and Ongi. Overnight accommodation is in standard ger camps positioned near each region's key sites; all meals and ground transportation between stages are included.
tour.highlights: ["Amarbayasgalant Monastery (built 1727), one of Mongolia's three major monastic centers, constructed without metal beams or nails", "Uran Togoo volcano crater (600 meters wide, 50–60 meters deep), dormant for 24,000 years, walkable into the caldera", "Khövsgöl Lake, 2,760 square kilometers, second-largest freshwater lake in Asia, bordered by Central Asian steppes and Siberian Taiga forests", "Tsaatan family visit — encounter the Dukha reindeer herders, one of Mongolia's most distinct ethnic groups", "Khorgo-Terkhiin Nuur National Park, including Terkhiin Tsagaan Lake (61 square kilometers) and dormant Khorgo volcano, shaped by eruption over 8,000 years ago", "Kharkhorin and Erdene Zuu Monastery (late 16th century), Mongolia's oldest Buddhist monastery, in the Orkhon Valley Cultural Landscape", "Ongi Monastery ruins, former home to over 2,000 monks, one of three major monastic centers in Mongolian history", "Bayanzag (Flaming Cliffs), site of the world's first discovered fossilized dinosaur eggs and Roy Chapman Andrews expeditions", "Khongor Sand Dunes (120 kilometers long, 6–12 kilometers wide), known as Singing Sand due to acoustics during wind and avalanches", "Yol Valley (Vulture Valley) in Gurvan Saikhan National Park, home to bearded vultures, Argali wild sheep, snow leopards, and seasonal ice glaciers", "Tsagaan Suvarga (White Stupa) cliffs with varied natural soil colors for photography", "Baga Gazarin Chuluu plateau with exotic granite rock formations and ruins of an ancient monastery destroyed in 1937"]
tour.itineraries:
Day 1 — Arrival in Ulaanbaatar
Arrive at Chinggis Khaan International Airport. The local team meets you for transfer to the city center, where you check into your hotel and gather for a welcome dinner.

Day 2 — Amarbayasgalant Monastery and the Road to Darkhan
Depart for Darkhan, one of Mongolia's two largest cities outside Ulaanbaatar, approximately 350 kilometers north. After lunch in Darkhan, continue toward Amarbayasgalant Monastery, reaching it in the late afternoon. Built in 1727 using traditional woodworking techniques, the monastery stands as one of the three major monastic centers in the country. Unlike most Mongolian monasteries damaged during the political purges of the 1930s, Amarbayasgalant survived in relatively intact condition—its construction contains no metal beams or nails. The surrounding monastic grounds and nearby hills offer meditative walking experiences. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 3 — Uran Togoo Volcano and Nomadic Family Visit
Journey to Uran Togoo, a dormant volcano that erupted approximately 24,000 years ago. The volcano sits within green steppes and forests, the largest of four dormant volcanoes in the surrounding valleys. The crater measures 600 meters wide and 50–60 meters deep, descending into a walkable caldera. The area offers trekking opportunities across volcanic terrain. After lunch in the town of Bulgan, visit a local nomadic family to observe traditional herding practices that have persisted and adapted into the modern era. Arrive at Sod Camp in the afternoon. The camp sits opposite a mountain range with trekking access and proximity to a mineral spring with reputed healing properties. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 4 — Khövsgöl Lake: Journey to Mongolia's Second-Largest Freshwater Lake
Travel approximately 350 kilometers northward to reach Lake Khövsgöl, the tour's primary destination. Stop for lunch near Moron, capital of Khövsgöl province, before continuing to the lakeshore camp. Khövsgöl spans 2,760 square kilometers and formed approximately two million years ago. The lake sits at the boundary between Central Asian steppes and Siberian Taiga forests, creating a distinct ecological zone. It is home to the Tsaatan people, also known as the Dukha, who sustain themselves primarily through reindeer herding and represent one of the country's most unique ethnic groups. Overnight in a standard ger camp (upgrade available).

Day 5 — Khövsgöl Lake: Optional Activities
A free day at the lake. Optional activities include boat rides on the water, horseback riding across surrounding terrain, visits to local nomadic families, excursions to Tsaatan reindeer herders' settlements, and trekking along shorelines and forest paths. Overnight in a standard ger camp (upgrades available).

Day 6 — Ulziit Khishig Camp
Depart in the morning toward Ulziit Khishig Camp, positioned 210 kilometers south along the route toward the tour's next destinations. The camp sits in a verdant valley surrounded by hillside forests. Overnight in a standard ger camp (cabin upgrade available).

Day 7 — Khorgo-Terkhiin Nuur National Park and Volcanic Crater Walk
Travel to Arkhangai province and Khorgo-Terkhiin Tsagaan Nuur National Park. The area centers on two landmarks: Terkhiin Tsagaan Lake, covering 61 square kilometers and home to numerous bird species, and the nearby dormant Khorgo volcano. The volcano erupted over 8,000 years ago; that eruption directly shaped the surrounding landscape and affected the formation of Terkhiin Tsagaan Lake. Visit the lake shores and trek to the volcano's crater rim for a panoramic view of the surrounding terrain. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 8 — Kharkhorin: Ancient Capital and Erdene Zuu Monastery
Drive toward Kharkhorin, located within the Orkhon Valley Cultural Landscape—a region where the history of Mongolia and the larger world took shape. Kharkhorin served as the capital of the Mongol Empire; the Kharkhorin Museum houses artifacts tracing origins to the Mongol dynasties and periods preceding them. The primary site visited is Erdene Zuu Monastery, the oldest Buddhist monastery in Mongolia, founded in the late 16th century. For centuries, thousands of monks inhabited this complex and shaped Mongolian cultural and artistic development. Political purges in the 1930s diminished its collections, but the monastic grounds were preserved. Both original temples and currently active temples remain accessible for visitation. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 9 — Ongi Monastery Ruins and Trek
Drive to the ruins of Ongi Monastery in Middle Gobi province, approximately 270 kilometers southeast. The monastery once stood on both banks of the Ongi River, from which it took its name. It ranks among the three major monastic centers in Mongolian history; at its peak, over 2,000 monks lived within its walls and shaped modern Mongolian art and culture. After lunch at the camp, trek the monastic grounds—currently undergoing gradual restoration—while learning its historical significance. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 10 — Bayanzag (Flaming Cliffs): Paleontology and Silk Road History
Drive approximately 190 kilometers to Bayanzag, known as the Flaming Cliffs for the fiery colors the rock face displays at sunset. The site holds significance both paleontologically and historically: it lies on the ancient Silk Road trade route and is where the world's first fossilized dinosaur eggs were discovered. After checking into camp and lunch, visit the local information center to learn about Roy Chapman Andrews's expeditions to the region—expeditions that inspired the character of Indiana Jones. The afternoon offers extensive trekking and photography opportunities across the Flaming Cliffs. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 11 — Khongor Sand Dunes: Singing Sand and Camel Trek
Drive approximately 170 kilometers to reach the Khongor Sand Dunes camp. After lunch and rest, visit a local nomadic family in the late afternoon and ride their camels to the dunes. The dunes are known locally as Singing Sand due to the distinctive sounds the sands produce during strong winds and avalanches. The dunes extend 120 kilometers in length and 6–12 kilometers in width. Trekking to the dune tops provides expansive views of the surrounding landscape. The Khongor River flows nearby, its water supporting local greenery and life. Overnight in a standard ger camp (upgrade available).

Day 12 — Yol Valley and Gurvan Saikhan National Park: Vultures and Wildlife
Travel approximately 220 kilometers toward Gurvan Saikhan National Park. Check into camp and have lunch, then depart for Yol Valley, nicknamed Vulture Valley for the bearded vultures that nest on the tall cliffs rising above 2,000 meters. The valley lies within Gurvan Saikhan National Park, home to Argali wild sheep, Ibex, snow leopards, and falcons; sightings depend on timing and luck. Yol Valley is also known for ice glaciers that form in winter and typically melt by early July. Trek through the valley with ample photography opportunities. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 13 — Tsagaan Suvarga (White Stupa): Colored Cliffs and Photography
Depart toward Middle Gobi to visit Tsagaan Suvarga—literally meaning White Stupa—named for the appearance of the local cliffs from a distance. Stop briefly in Mandalgobi for lunch. Upon arrival, check into the local camp and enjoy a relaxed afternoon. The cliffs can be visited in the late afternoon and again the following morning. The local soil composition creates varied natural colors across the rock face, making the site a notable destination for photography. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 14 — Baga Gazarin Chuluu: Granite Formations and Monastery Ruins
Depart toward Baga Gazarin Chuluu, a plateau characterized by exotic granite rock formations. After checking into the local ger camp and lunch, visit the ruins of an ancient monastery destroyed during the political purges of 1937. Walk among the rock formations themselves; the area offers trekking opportunities across distinctive terrain. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 15 — Return to Ulaanbaatar
220-kilometer drive.

output.name: Mongolia: Khövsgöl to the Gobi — 15 Days
output.subtitle: A north-to-south private journey from Asia's great freshwater lake to the Flaming Cliffs and singing dunes of the Gobi, moving through volcanic highlands, ancient capitals, and monastic ruins
output.summary:
This journey traces a deliberate arc from the subarctic shore of Lake Khövsgöl to the ochre silence of the Gobi Desert, crossing a landscape that holds some of the most significant cultural and geological formations on earth. It is not a circuit of highlights; it is a layered reading of a country whose history, terrain, and living traditions reward careful attention.

The route moves through volcanic highlands and glacial valleys, along the banks of the Orkhon River where the Mongol Empire once centered its world, past the ruins of monasteries that shaped Mongolian art and thought before being silenced in the purges of the 1930s. At Amarbayasgalant — built in 1727 without a single metal beam or nail — and at Erdene Zuu, Mongolia's oldest surviving Buddhist monastery, time and craftsmanship are visible in every detail. The Ongi Monastery ruins, set on both banks of a quiet river, carry a different register: the weight of what was lost.

Northward, Lake Khövsgöl offers an entirely different kind of stillness — two million years old, bordered by Siberian taiga and Central Asian steppe, home to the Dukha, a small community of reindeer herders whose way of life is unlike anything else in the country. Time at the lake is unhurried, preference-led, and guided with an understanding that some places are best encountered without agenda.

In the Gobi, the scale shifts. The Khongor Sand Dunes stretch 120 kilometers. Bayanzag — the Flaming Cliffs — glows at the hour when the light is right. Yol Valley, set within Gurvan Saikhan National Park, narrows between cliffs rising above 2,000 meters, sheltering bearded vultures and, in the right season, ice formations in the valley floor. Throughout, ger camps are positioned close to each region's key sites, chosen for their setting and privacy. Atlas & Hearth shapes each stage so that demanding travel days are balanced by considered pacing, and every cultural encounter is given time to be understood rather than simply witnessed.

output.itineraries:
Day 1 — Arrival in Ulaanbaatar
Arrive at Chinggis Khaan International Airport, where the team meets you for a private transfer into the city. The evening is yours to settle in before a welcome dinner.

Day 2 — Amarbayasgalant Monastery: A 1727 Monastic Masterwork
The journey north begins early, covering roughly 350 kilometers to Darkhan before continuing toward Amarbayasgalant Monastery, reached in the late afternoon when the light is low and the grounds are quiet. Built in 1727, the monastery represents one of the three great monastic centers of Mongolia and one of its most remarkable feats of craftsmanship — the entire structure was raised without a single metal beam or nail. Where most Mongolian monasteries were severely damaged during the political purges of the 1930s, Amarbayasgalant survived in largely intact condition. A private guiding session here is unhurried; the surrounding hills and monastic grounds reward walking and quiet observation in equal measure. The night is spent at a ger camp positioned near the monastery.

Day 3 — Uran Togoo Crater Walk and Nomadic Family Visit near Bulgan
The morning moves through green steppes and forest toward Uran Togoo, the largest of four dormant volcanoes in the surrounding valleys and one that has been silent for approximately 24,000 years. Its crater — 600 meters wide and 50 to 60 meters deep — is entirely walkable, and descending into the caldera gives a particular sense of the geological forces that shaped this region. The volcanic terrain invites trekking at your own pace. After a midday stop in the town of Bulgan, the afternoon brings a visit to a local nomadic family — an opportunity to observe herding practices that have both persisted and adapted across generations, explained through expert guiding rather than performance. The camp at Sod sits opposite a mountain range with trekking access and proximity to a mineral spring the locals hold in some regard. The ger accommodation here is comfortable and well-positioned for the evening's quiet.

Day 4 — Lake Khövsgöl: Arrival at Mongolia's Great Northern Water
The drive to Lake Khövsgöl covers approximately 350 kilometers northward, with a lunch stop near Moron, the provincial capital. The lake itself is ancient — formed around two million years ago — and its setting is unlike anywhere else in Mongolia. At 2,760 square kilometers, it sits precisely at the ecological boundary between Central Asian steppe and Siberian taiga, creating a transition zone that shapes both the landscape and the people who have lived beside it. The Dukha, also known as the Tsaatan, sustain themselves through reindeer herding and represent one of the country's most distinct communities. The lakeshore camp is chosen for its privacy and proximity to the water. The remainder of the day is spent settling in and taking the measure of a place that merits more than a glance.

Day 5 — Lake Khövsgöl: A Day Shaped by Your Interests
A full day at leisure by the water. Pursue boat rides, horseback excursions across the surrounding terrain, visits to nomadic families, or treks along shorelines and forest paths. The pace remains unhurried, the camp your comfortable base. Expert guidance is available throughout.

Day 6 — Southward to Ulziit Khishig Camp in the Valley
The route turns south, traveling approximately 210 kilometers toward the journey's next destinations. Ulziit Khishig Camp sits in a green valley enclosed by forested hillsides — a composed and private setting that offers a natural point of rest between the lake's expansive openness and the volcanic highlands ahead. The evening here is quiet.

Day 7 — Khorgo Volcano Crater Rim and Terkhiin Tsagaan Lake
The day centers on Khorgo-Terkhiin Tsagaan Nuur National Park in Arkhangai province, an area shaped by volcanic forces more than 8,000 years ago. The eruption of Khorgo volcano directly influenced the formation of Terkhiin Tsagaan Lake, which covers 61 square kilometers and supports a notable variety of bird life along its shores. The afternoon moves between the lakeshore and the volcano itself — trekking to the crater rim opens a panorama of the park's layered terrain: lava fields, wetlands, and the wide arc of the lake below. Expert guiding places the geology and ecology in a wider regional narrative. Overnight in a ger camp positioned within the park.

Day 8 — Kharkhorin and Erdene Zuu: The Orkhon Valley's Imperial Memory
Few landscapes in Asia carry the historical weight of the Orkhon Valley. Kharkhorin served as the capital of the Mongol Empire — a city that, at its height, drew diplomats, merchants, and scholars from across the known world. The Kharkhorin Museum presents artifacts and context tracing the site's significance through Mongol imperial history and the periods that preceded it. The primary visit is Erdene Zuu Monastery, founded in the late 16th century and considered Mongolia's oldest surviving Buddhist monastery. For several centuries, its complex housed thousands of monks whose work shaped the country's cultural and artistic traditions. The purges of the 1930s took a severe toll on its collections, yet the monastic grounds survived. Both original and currently active temples remain open for private visitation, and the guiding here is particularly attentive to the fine detail of architecture, iconography, and continuity. Overnight in a ger camp in the valley.

Day 9 — Ongi Monastery Ruins: Silence on the Banks of the Ongi River
The drive southeast — approximately 270 kilometers into Middle Gobi province — brings the journey to the ruins of Ongi Monastery, one of the three great monastic centers in Mongolian history. The complex once occupied both banks of the Ongi River and, at its height, sheltered more than 2,000 monks whose contributions to Mongolian art and culture were considerable. The political purges of the 1930s left the site in ruin; gradual restoration is ongoing. Walking the grounds with expert guiding — understanding what stood here, what was lost, and what is slowly returning — is a more affecting experience than any summary of the site suggests. The afternoon is shaped around that walk and the contemplative atmosphere the riverbanks carry.

Day 10 — Bayanzag: The Flaming Cliffs and Their Paleontological Significance
The drive of approximately 190 kilometers delivers the journey to Bayanzag — the Flaming Cliffs — named for the color the rock face takes when the light falls at the right angle. The site carries two distinct registers of significance: it lies along the ancient Silk Road trade route, and it is where the world's first fossilized dinosaur eggs were discovered. The local information center offers a considered account of the Roy Chapman Andrews expeditions that brought Bayanzag to international attention — expeditions whose spirit, it has often been noted, informed the fictional character of Indiana Jones. The afternoon is given over to walking the cliffs at the hour when their colors are most vivid. Expert guiding here connects the paleontological record to the broader geological history of the Gobi, lending the landscape an intellectual as well as visual depth.

Day 11 — Khongor Sand Dunes: The Singing Sand of the Gobi
The approach to the Khongor Sand Dunes — a drive of approximately 170 kilometers — marks a shift in the landscape's register. The dunes extend 120 kilometers in length and between 6 and 12 kilometers in width; they are known locally as Singing Sand for the distinctive resonance the sands produce under strong wind and during avalanche. The late afternoon brings a visit to a local nomadic family whose camels provide the most natural way to approach the dunes across the flat ground — a mode of travel that feels appropriate to the terrain and to the pace that the Gobi asks of its visitors. Trekking to the dune crests opens a wide view of the surrounding desert floor and the thin green line of the Khongor River, whose water sustains the vegetation at the dunes' base. The accommodation here is positioned close to the dunes, and the evening quiet is considerable.

Day 12 — Yol Valley and Gurvan Saikhan National Park: Cliffs, Vultures, and Ice
The drive of approximately 220 kilometers into Gurvan Saikhan National Park brings the journey to Yol Valley — known as Vulture Valley for the bearded vultures that nest on cliffs rising above 2,000 meters. What is consistent is the valley's atmosphere: narrow, high-walled, and geologically distinct. Ice formations develop here through winter and typically persist into early July on the valley floor. The afternoon is given to a guided walk through the valley at a considered pace, with attention to the ecology and the particular quietness the terrain produces. Overnight in a well-positioned ger camp within the park.

Day 13 — Tsagaan Suvarga: The White Stupa Cliffs of Middle Gobi
The route moves toward Tsagaan Suvarga — literally White Stupa, named for the formation's resemblance, from a distance, to a Buddhist structure. A midday stop in Mandalgobi breaks the drive before arrival at the local camp. The cliffs draw their character from the varied mineral composition of the soil, which produces bands of shifting natural color across the rock face — particularly visible in the late afternoon. The evening is unhurried; the cliffs reward a second visit in the early morning, and the itinerary allows for both.

Day 14 — Baga Gazarin Chuluu: Granite Formations and a Monastery Lost in 1937
The granite plateau of Baga Gazarin Chuluu presents a landscape of striking rock formations and historical layering. After settling into the local ger camp, the afternoon visit takes in the ruins of an ancient monastery destroyed during the 1937 purges — a site that echoes Ongi in its register of loss — alongside the rock formations themselves, which reward unhurried walking and careful observation. The terrain is distinctive, and the guiding here draws out the connection between the natural landscape and the human history embedded within it.

Day 15 — Return to Ulaanbaatar
A 220-kilometer drive concludes the journey.

tour.itineraries:
Day 1 — Arrival in Ulaanbaatar
Arrive at Chinggis Khaan International Airport. The local team meets you for transfer to the city center, where you check into your hotel and gather for a welcome dinner.

Day 2 — Amarbayasgalant Monastery and the Road to Darkhan
Depart for Darkhan, one of Mongolia's two largest cities outside Ulaanbaatar, approximately 350 kilometers north. After lunch in Darkhan, continue toward Amarbayasgalant Monastery, reaching it in the late afternoon. Built in 1727 using traditional woodworking techniques, the monastery stands as one of the three major monastic centers in the country. Unlike most Mongolian monasteries damaged during the political purges of the 1930s, Amarbayasgalant survived in relatively intact condition—its construction contains no metal beams or nails. The surrounding monastic grounds and nearby hills offer meditative walking experiences. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 3 — Uran Togoo Volcano and Nomadic Family Visit
Journey to Uran Togoo, a dormant volcano that erupted approximately 24,000 years ago. The volcano sits within green steppes and forests, the largest of four dormant volcanoes in the surrounding valleys. The crater measures 600 meters wide and 50–60 meters deep, descending into a walkable caldera. The area offers trekking opportunities across volcanic terrain. After lunch in the town of Bulgan, visit a local nomadic family to observe traditional herding practices that have persisted and adapted into the modern era. Arrive at Sod Camp in the afternoon. The camp sits opposite a mountain range with trekking access and proximity to a mineral spring with reputed healing properties. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 4 — Khövsgöl Lake: Journey to Mongolia's Second-Largest Freshwater Lake
Travel approximately 350 kilometers northward to reach Lake Khövsgöl, the tour's primary destination. Stop for lunch near Moron, capital of Khövsgöl province, before continuing to the lakeshore camp. Khövsgöl spans 2,760 square kilometers and formed approximately two million years ago. The lake sits at the boundary between Central Asian steppes and Siberian Taiga forests, creating a distinct ecological zone. It is home to the Tsaatan people, also known as the Dukha, who sustain themselves primarily through reindeer herding and represent one of the country's most unique ethnic groups. Overnight in a standard ger camp (upgrade available).

Day 5 — Khövsgöl Lake: Optional Activities
A free day at the lake. Optional activities include boat rides on the water, horseback riding across surrounding terrain, visits to local nomadic families, excursions to Tsaatan reindeer herders' settlements, and trekking along shorelines and forest paths. Overnight in a standard ger camp (upgrades available).

Day 6 — Ulziit Khishig Camp
Depart in the morning toward Ulziit Khishig Camp, positioned 210 kilometers south along the route toward the tour's next destinations. The camp sits in a verdant valley surrounded by hillside forests. Overnight in a standard ger camp (cabin upgrade available).

Day 7 — Khorgo-Terkhiin Nuur National Park and Volcanic Crater Walk
Travel to Arkhangai province and Khorgo-Terkhiin Tsagaan Nuur National Park. The area centers on two landmarks: Terkhiin Tsagaan Lake, covering 61 square kilometers and home to numerous bird species, and the nearby dormant Khorgo volcano. The volcano erupted over 8,000 years ago; that eruption directly shaped the surrounding landscape and affected the formation of Terkhiin Tsagaan Lake. Visit the lake shores and trek to the volcano's crater rim for a panoramic view of the surrounding terrain. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 8 — Kharkhorin: Ancient Capital and Erdene Zuu Monastery
Drive toward Kharkhorin, located within the Orkhon Valley Cultural Landscape—a region where the history of Mongolia and the larger world took shape. Kharkhorin served as the capital of the Mongol Empire; the Kharkhorin Museum houses artifacts tracing origins to the Mongol dynasties and periods preceding them. The primary site visited is Erdene Zuu Monastery, the oldest Buddhist monastery in Mongolia, founded in the late 16th century. For centuries, thousands of monks inhabited this complex and shaped Mongolian cultural and artistic development. Political purges in the 1930s diminished its collections, but the monastic grounds were preserved. Both original temples and currently active temples remain accessible for visitation. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 9 — Ongi Monastery Ruins and Trek
Drive to the ruins of Ongi Monastery in Middle Gobi province, approximately 270 kilometers southeast. The monastery once stood on both banks of the Ongi River, from which it took its name. It ranks among the three major monastic centers in Mongolian history; at its peak, over 2,000 monks lived within its walls and shaped modern Mongolian art and culture. After lunch at the camp, trek the monastic grounds—currently undergoing gradual restoration—while learning its historical significance. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 10 — Bayanzag (Flaming Cliffs): Paleontology and Silk Road History
Drive approximately 190 kilometers to Bayanzag, known as the Flaming Cliffs for the fiery colors the rock face displays at sunset. The site holds significance both paleontologically and historically: it lies on the ancient Silk Road trade route and is where the world's first fossilized dinosaur eggs were discovered. After checking into camp and lunch, visit the local information center to learn about Roy Chapman Andrews's expeditions to the region—expeditions that inspired the character of Indiana Jones. The afternoon offers extensive trekking and photography opportunities across the Flaming Cliffs. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 11 — Khongor Sand Dunes: Singing Sand and Camel Trek
Drive approximately 170 kilometers to reach the Khongor Sand Dunes camp. After lunch and rest, visit a local nomadic family in the late afternoon and ride their camels to the dunes. The dunes are known locally as Singing Sand due to the distinctive sounds the sands produce during strong winds and avalanches. The dunes extend 120 kilometers in length and 6–12 kilometers in width. Trekking to the dune tops provides expansive views of the surrounding landscape. The Khongor River flows nearby, its water supporting local greenery and life. Overnight in a standard ger camp (upgrade available).

Day 12 — Yol Valley and Gurvan Saikhan National Park: Vultures and Wildlife
Travel approximately 220 kilometers toward Gurvan Saikhan National Park. Check into camp and have lunch, then depart for Yol Valley, nicknamed Vulture Valley for the bearded vultures that nest on the tall cliffs rising above 2,000 meters. The valley lies within Gurvan Saikhan National Park, home to Argali wild sheep, Ibex, snow leopards, and falcons; sightings depend on timing and luck. Yol Valley is also known for ice glaciers that form in winter and typically melt by early July. Trek through the valley with ample photography opportunities. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 13 — Tsagaan Suvarga (White Stupa): Colored Cliffs and Photography
Depart toward Middle Gobi to visit Tsagaan Suvarga—literally meaning White Stupa—named for the appearance of the local cliffs from a distance. Stop briefly in Mandalgobi for lunch. Upon arrival, check into the local camp and enjoy a relaxed afternoon. The cliffs can be visited in the late afternoon and again the following morning. The local soil composition creates varied natural colors across the rock face, making the site a notable destination for photography. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 14 — Baga Gazarin Chuluu: Granite Formations and Monastery Ruins
Depart toward Baga Gazarin Chuluu, a plateau characterized by exotic granite rock formations. After checking into the local ger camp and lunch, visit the ruins of an ancient monastery destroyed during the political purges of 1937. Walk among the rock formations themselves; the area offers trekking opportunities across distinctive terrain. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 15 — Return to Ulaanbaatar
220-kilometer drive.

output.subtitle: A north-to-south family journey from Asia's second-largest freshwater lake through ancient monastic sites to the Gobi's Flaming Cliffs and Singing Dunes
output.summary:
This 15-day journey traces a north-to-south arc through Mongolia's most distinct landscapes and historical centers, paced to suit families traveling with children aged 7–16. The route begins at Khövsgöl Lake — 2,760 square kilometers of freshwater bordered by Central Asian steppe and Siberian taiga — where families can meet the Tsaatan reindeer herders of the Dukha people before moving south through volcanic terrain, ancient monastic complexes, and the wide open Orkhon Valley. The final stage crosses into the Gobi Desert, taking in the paleontological landmark of Bayanzag, the acoustically distinctive Khongor Sand Dunes, and the wildlife terrain of Gurvan Saikhan National Park.

Each day is structured to give families both active discovery and adequate rest. Long driving stages — several exceed 200 kilometers — are built into the schedule as natural transition days with roadside stops and time to settle into each ger camp before activities begin. Guides are present throughout to frame the educational dimensions of each site, from dinosaur fossil history to nomadic culture, in ways that engage children without reducing the experience to a classroom exercise. Overnight accommodation throughout is in ger camps positioned near each region's key sites; all meals and ground transportation between stages are included.

The pace across 15 days allows families to absorb Mongolia's scale — the silence of volcanic craters, the color of the Flaming Cliffs at dusk, the sound of wind across the sand dunes — without the journey feeling rushed or relentless.

Day 11 — Khongor Sand Dunes: Camel Riding and the Singing Sands of the Gobi

Walking to the dune tops provides wide views across the surrounding Gobi terrain. The Khongor River flows nearby, its water sustaining a strip of greenery visible from the dunes. Day 12 — Yol Valley Wildlife Walk in Gurvan Saikhan National Park
A drive of approximately 220 kilometers leads toward Gurvan Saikhan National Park. After checking into camp and having lunch, families depart for Yol Valley — known as Vulture Valley — where bearded vultures nest on cliff faces rising above 2,000 meters. tour.itineraries:
Day 1 — Arrival at Samdrup Jongkhar Border Gate
Arrive at Gauwahati Airport and drive 98km to Samdrup Jongkhar. Clear immigration formalities, then check into your hotel.

Day 2 — Tashigang: Bamboo Forests, Battlefield & Handlooms
A 180-kilometer drive eastward through bamboo countryside leads to Tashigang. Visit Dewathang's historical battlefield, visit Khaling National Handloom, then Chorten Kora. Evening spent at a local home experiencing traditional cooking.

Day 3 — Mongar Dzong & Traditional Ara Brewing
Drive to Mongar (90km, 3 hours). Visit Mongar Dzong, then lunch at a local farmhouse to taste traditional eastern dishes and observe ara—corn liquor—being brewed.

Day 4 — Bumthang: Lakes, Villages & Sacred Temples
The 190-kilometer drive to Bumthang takes five hours through mountain passes. Stop at Mebar Tsho Lake, then continue to Ura Village for lunch of puta—buckwheat noodles. Afternoon visits to Kurje Lhakhang and Jambay Lhakhang, two of Bhutan's most significant temples.

Day 5 — Punakha: River Valleys & the Fortress Dzong
The six-hour drive descends through green valleys to Punakha. Lunch by the riverside features Bhutanese-style river trout and red and white rice. Evening visit to Punakha Dzong.

Day 6 — Thimphu: Buddha Statue, Zoo & Traditional Crafts
Drive to Thimphu via Dochu La Pass (74km, 2hrs). Visit Kuenselphodrang to see Asia's tallest bronze Buddha statue. Lunch at Babesa village, then visit the Takin Zoo, National Library, and Traditional School of Arts and Craft.

Day 7 — Thimphu Textiles, Markets & Dumplings
Visit the Textile Museum, Craft Bazaar, and Kaja Throm Farmers Market. Lunch at a traditional dumpling house. Afternoon free.

Day 8 — Paro: Drive and Tiger's Nest Monastery Trek
Drive to Paro. Trek to Tiger's Nest Monastery in Paro.

Day 9 — Paro: Temples, Museum & Local Brewery
Visit Kyichu Lhakhang and Ta Dzong National Museum in the morning. Lunch features local rice pizza and buckwheat dumplings with dried spinach. Afternoon includes a brewery tour and stroll through Paro town.

Day 10 — Departure from Your Hotel
Check out and depart for the airport.

output.subtitle: Samdrup Jongkhar to Paro via Tashigang, Bumthang, and Thimphu — farmhouse cooking, sacred temples, and a family-paced route through Bhutan's mountain heartland
output.summary:
This ten-day journey crosses Bhutan from its eastern border to Paro in the west, tracing a route through valleys, mountain passes, and historic towns that most visitors to the country never reach. For families, the itinerary's real strength is in how it builds understanding rather than simply accumulating sights. Children encounter food as a living record of each region — buckwheat noodles at a high-altitude village restaurant in Bumthang, river trout prepared by the Punakha riverside, dumplings at a traditional house in Thimphu — while adults gain context through farmhouse visits, weaving workshops, and a working brewery in Paro. Sacred temples in Bumthang, the riverside fortress of Punakha Dzong, and the challenging but rewarding climb to Tiger's Nest Monastery give the route cultural weight without making every day feel structured around formal learning.

Long mountain drives are unavoidable in Bhutan, and this itinerary does not pretend otherwise. Several days involve journeys of between three and six hours on roads that wind through forested passes and river valleys. English-speaking guides manage these transitions, using stops and natural breaks to keep the pace manageable. Accommodation is half-board throughout, with private vehicle transfers, which reduces decision fatigue for families. On days with longer drives, afternoon activities are deliberately lighter. The Tiger's Nest trek on Day 8 is the most physically demanding element, involving a steep ascent to approximately 3,120 metres; the guide can advise on pace, and families with younger or less confident walkers can set their own turning point on the trail. The overall structure alternates between active cultural days and gentler ones, making the journey engaging for children across a range of ages while remaining practical for parents.

output.itineraries:
Day 1 — Arrival at Samdrup Jongkhar — Eastern Border Entry
The journey begins at Guwahati Airport in India, followed by a 98-kilometre road transfer to Samdrup Jongkhar on Bhutan's eastern border. After clearing immigration formalities, the group checks into the hotel for the night.

Day 2 — Tashigang: Bamboo Countryside, Handloom Weaving & a Village Evening
A 180-kilometre drive through bamboo-forested hills leads to Tashigang, one of Bhutan's easternmost towns. Along the way, the route passes Dewathang's historical battlefield. In Tashigang, a visit to the Khaling National Handloom centre offers children a close look at traditional weaving techniques, with weavers working at floor looms in a setting that makes the craft easy to observe. Chorten Kora, a large white stupa near the Dangme Chhu river, is visited before the evening, which is spent at a local home where families experience eastern Bhutanese cooking firsthand.

Day 3 — Mongar Dzong & Traditional Ara Brewing
Drive to Mongar (90km, 3 hours). Visit the whitewashed Mongar Dzong fortress-monastery overlooking the town. Lunch at a local farmhouse features eastern Bhutanese dishes and a demonstration of traditional ara—corn liquor—brewing.

Day 4 — Bumthang: Mebar Tsho Lake, Ura Village & Sacred Temples
The 190-kilometre drive to Bumthang crosses several mountain passes and takes around five hours. The guide uses natural rest stops along the way to keep the journey manageable. En route, the group pauses at Mebar Tsho — a lake set in a steep, forested gorge with significant religious importance in Bhutanese Buddhism. Lunch in Ura Village introduces families to puta, the region's buckwheat noodle dish, served at a local restaurant and suitable for all ages. The afternoon includes visits to Kurje Lhakhang and Jambay Lhakhang, two of Bhutan's oldest and most revered temples in the Bumthang valley, where guides provide age-appropriate context for younger visitors.

Day 5 — Punakha: River Valley Drive & Fortress Dzong
A six-hour descent through green river valleys brings the group to Punakha. Lunch is taken by the riverside, featuring Bhutanese-style river trout and red and white rice — a straightforward meal that works well for families with varied preferences. The evening visit to Punakha Dzong, a seventeenth-century fortress set at the confluence of two rivers, provides a natural end to a long travel day without adding further demands on energy.

Day 6 — Thimphu: Buddha Statue, Takin Zoo & Traditional Arts School
The 74-kilometre drive to Thimphu crosses Dochu La Pass, with a brief stop possible for views over the valley. At Kuenselphodrang, the group walks through landscaped gardens to reach Asia's largest bronze Buddha statue. Lunch is taken in Babesa village. The afternoon includes a visit to the Takin Zoo, home to Bhutan's national animal, followed by the National Library and the Traditional School of Arts and Craft, where students work across painting, weaving, and woodcarving — a setting that children and adults tend to find equally engaging.

Day 7 — Thimphu Textiles, Markets & Dumplings
Visit the Textile Museum and Craft Bazaar, then browse Kaja Throm Farmers Market. Lunch at a traditional dumpling house. Afternoon free.

Day 8 — Paro: Drive and Tiger's Nest Monastery Trek
Drive to Paro, then trek to Tiger's Nest Monastery, a clifftop temple perched at 3,120 metres. The steep ascent takes two to three hours each way.

Day 9 — Paro: Temples, National Museum & a Local Brewery
The morning begins at Kyichu Lhakhang, one of Bhutan's oldest temples, followed by Ta Dzong, the former watchtower that now houses the National Museum, with collections covering natural history, textiles, and Bhutanese art. Lunch features local rice pizza and buckwheat dumplings with dried spinach — dishes that introduce children to the regional pantry in a familiar format. The afternoon includes a tour of a working brewery in Paro, providing adult cultural context on local production, followed by a walk through Paro town.

Day 10 — Paro: Departure from Hotel
The tour concludes with checkout and a transfer to the airport.

tour.name: Laos to Vietnam by Bicycle: Nam Ou River to Hanoi — 12 Days
tour.subtitle: A 12-day cycling route from Luang Prabang through the Nam Ou valley and across the Vietnam border to Hanoi, combining tarmac and dirt-road riding with village stays and a river boat journey.
tour.summary: This 12-day cycling route connects Laos and Vietnam by bicycle and boat, covering mixed terrain. The journey begins in Luang Prabang, follows the Nam Ou River valley northward, crosses into Vietnam at Muang Khua, and descends through northern Vietnamese provinces to Cuc Phuong National Park and Hanoi. Days combine road cycling (ranging from 40 to 80 kilometers) with trekking sections, village homestays, and a boat journey through the Nam Ou gorge. Terrain includes tarmac roads, unpaved mountain tracks, and riverside routes; elevation varies from sea level to approximately 1,450 meters. The route passes through communities of Khmu, Hmong, Tai, and Black Tai populations, with accommodation split between hotels, guesthouses, and family homestays. This is a physically demanding itinerary requiring cycling fitness and tolerance for basic accommodation.

tour.itineraries:
Day 1 — Arrival and Orientation Cycling in Luang Prabang
Meet the guide and team upon arrival in Luang Prabang. A short sunset ride around the town provides acclimatization and a gauge of fitness levels before the journey begins. An informal briefing and dinner follow at Khaiphaen Restaurant, a vocational training establishment. Overnight in Luang Prabang.

Day 2 — Kuang Si Waterfalls and Trek to Ban Long Lao Mai
Depart early by bicycle on the mountain road leading south from Luang Prabang to Kuang Si Waterfalls, approximately 30 kilometers on tarmac. The falls feature turquoise pools suitable for swimming. After lunch—Laos-style grilled meat and vegetables—leave bicycles behind and trek through forest to Ban Long Lao Mai, a village where Khmu families and Hmong residents, resettled by the government following the end of Laos's civil war, now live. The two communities historically occupied distinct territories; integration occurred gradually over decades. Dinner is shared with a homestay family. Overnight in Ban Long Lao Mai.

Day 3 — Jungle Trek from Ban Long Lao Mai to Nong Khouay
Breakfast with the homestay family begins the day. A 9-kilometer trek through the valley over approximately 3 hours brings you to Nong Khouay, a village without grid electricity or mobile signal. The small central shop serves as a gathering point. Villagers are accustomed to visitors and offer conversation over coffee or beer. In the evening, a village elder may share local history and observations. Overnight in Nong Khouay.

Day 4 — Cycling the Nam Ou Valley to Nong Khiaw
A one-hour descent on dirt road leads to the start of the northbound cycling route. The route skirts the Nam Ou River valley, passing Pak Mong village where lunch occurs, before entering an area of tall limestone karst formations. The landscape shifts noticeably as the valley narrows and elevation rises. Terrain includes dirt and tarmac sections. Total distance is approximately 80 kilometers. Overnight in Nong Khiaw.

Day 5 — Nam Ou River Boat Journey to Muang Khua
A 4–5 hour boat ride travels upriver through the Nam Ou gorge to Muang Khua. The river route passes primary forest on both banks and includes stops at remote villages accessible only by water. Overnight in Muang Khua.

Day 6 — Cycling Through Primary Forest to the Laos–Vietnam Border and Dien Bien Phu
A 60-kilometer cycling day crosses from Laos into Vietnam. Much of the route runs through primary forest; the road surface combines tarmac and unpaved sections. The route passes through villages of hill-tribe communities. At the border, a Vietnamese guide takes over transport to Dien Bien Phu, located in the Muong Thanh Valley. The city is known internationally as the site of a battle that marked the end of French colonial rule in Indochina. The valley is also known for wet rice cultivation and Tai ethnic dance traditions. Overnight in Dien Bien Phu.

Day 7 — Cycling Through Tai Communities to Tuan Giao
An 80-kilometer cycle through villages populated primarily by Tai ethnic groups leads to Tuan Giao. One significant climb occurs at a mountain pass approximately 15 kilometers outside Dien Bien Phu. Overall terrain is considered moderate. Overnight in a guesthouse in Tuan Giao.

Day 8 — Pha Din Pass Descent and Cycling to Son La
A short vehicle transfer ascends to Pha Din Pass (known locally as the "Heaven and Earth" pass), situated at approximately 1,450 meters. From the summit, a 15-kilometer downhill section descends through green rice fields and karst valleys with minimal traffic. The descent passes through areas where Tai and Hmong communities live, with agricultural activity visible throughout. Total cycling distance from the pass to Son La is significant. Overnight in a hotel in Son La.

Day 9 — Gradual Descent Through Rice Terraces to Moc Chau
A short vehicle transfer precedes a 45-kilometer cycling day with gentle downhill gradient. The route runs beneath limestone cliffs and through terraced rice paddies. Afternoon cycling passes through agricultural landscapes dominated by rice cultivation. Overnight in Moc Chau.

Day 10 — Black Tai Communities and Tea Plantations to Mai Chau
A 45-kilometer cycling day on quiet back roads enters territory primarily inhabited by Black Tai (Tai Dam) communities. As elevation rises to approximately 1,000 meters near Mai Chau, the landscape transitions to include plum orchards, corn fields, and tea plantations. Road surfaces are narrow and receive light traffic. Overnight in a homestay in Mai Chau.

Day 11 — Ma River Valley Cycling and Transfer to Cuc Phuong National Park
An 80-kilometer cycling day follows the Ma River through working agricultural land where subsistence farming and crop cultivation remain visible throughout. In late afternoon, a vehicle transfer takes you to Cuc Phuong National Park, Vietnam's important nature reserve containing the country's largest area of primary forest. A visit to the Primate Rescue Centre provides information on species recovery efforts, including the Cat Ba Langur, one of the world's most endangered primates. Overnight in a park bungalow.

Day 12 — Final Cycling Through Cuc Phuong Forest to Hanoi
A final 40-kilometer cycling section traverses Cuc Phuong forest to the park center. After a tea break, a vehicle transfer completes the journey to Hanoi. Guide and driver support is available for the final leg. End of services.

tour.name: Mongolia: Khövsgöl Lake and Gobi Desert — 15 Days
tour.subtitle: From the Siberian Taiga forests of Khövsgöl Lake to the Gobi's Flaming Cliffs and sand dunes, crossing Mongolia's northern steppes and central plateaus.
tour.summary: This 15-day itinerary traces a north-to-south arc through Mongolia's distinct ecosystems and historical centers. The route begins at Khövsgöl Lake, Asia's second-largest freshwater lake and home to the Tsaatan reindeer herders, then moves through volcanic regions and ancient monastic sites before descending into the Gobi Desert. The journey encounters dormant volcanoes, paleontological landmarks, granite rock formations, and the layered ruins of centers that shaped Mongolian culture—from the 13th-century capital Kharkhorin to the now-silent monastic complexes of Amarbayasgalant, Erdene Zuu, and Ongi. Overnight accommodation is in standard ger camps positioned near each region's key sites; all meals and ground transportation between stages are included.

tour.itineraries:
Day 1 — Arrival in Ulaanbaatar
Arrive at Chinggis Khaan International Airport. The local team meets you for transfer to the city center, where you check into your hotel and gather for a welcome dinner.

Day 2 — Amarbayasgalant Monastery and the Road to Darkhan
Depart for Darkhan, one of Mongolia's two largest cities outside Ulaanbaatar, approximately 350 kilometers north. After lunch in Darkhan, continue toward Amarbayasgalant Monastery, reaching it in the late afternoon. Built in 1727 using traditional woodworking techniques, the monastery stands as one of the three major monastic centers in the country. Unlike most Mongolian monasteries damaged during the political purges of the 1930s, Amarbayasgalant survived in relatively intact condition—its construction contains no metal beams or nails. The surrounding monastic grounds and nearby hills offer meditative walking experiences. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 3 — Uran Togoo Volcano and Nomadic Family Visit
Journey to Uran Togoo, a dormant volcano that erupted approximately 24,000 years ago. The volcano sits within green steppes and forests, the largest of four dormant volcanoes in the surrounding valleys. The crater measures 600 meters wide and 50–60 meters deep, descending into a walkable caldera. The area offers trekking opportunities across volcanic terrain. After lunch in the town of Bulgan, visit a local nomadic family to observe traditional herding practices that have persisted and adapted into the modern era. Arrive at Sod Camp in the afternoon. The camp sits opposite a mountain range with trekking access and proximity to a mineral spring with reputed healing properties. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 4 — Khövsgöl Lake: Journey to Mongolia's Second-Largest Freshwater Lake
Travel approximately 350 kilometers northward to reach Lake Khövsgöl, the tour's primary destination. Stop for lunch near Moron, capital of Khövsgöl province, before continuing to the lakeshore camp. Khövsgöl spans 2,760 square kilometers and formed approximately two million years ago. The lake sits at the boundary between Central Asian steppes and Siberian Taiga forests, creating a distinct ecological zone. It is home to the Tsaatan people, also known as the Dukha, who sustain themselves primarily through reindeer herding and represent one of the country's most unique ethnic groups. Overnight in a standard ger camp (upgrade available).

Day 5 — Khövsgöl Lake: Optional Activities
A free day at the lake. Optional activities include boat rides on the water, horseback riding across surrounding terrain, visits to local nomadic families, excursions to Tsaatan reindeer herders' settlements, and trekking along shorelines and forest paths. Overnight in a standard ger camp (upgrades available).

Day 6 — Ulziit Khishig Camp
Depart in the morning toward Ulziit Khishig Camp, positioned 210 kilometers south along the route toward the tour's next destinations. The camp sits in a verdant valley surrounded by hillside forests. Overnight in a standard ger camp (cabin upgrade available).

Day 7 — Khorgo-Terkhiin Nuur National Park and Volcanic Crater Walk
Travel to Arkhangai province and Khorgo-Terkhiin Tsagaan Nuur National Park. The area centers on two landmarks: Terkhiin Tsagaan Lake, covering 61 square kilometers and home to numerous bird species, and the nearby dormant Khorgo volcano. The volcano erupted over 8,000 years ago; that eruption directly shaped the surrounding landscape and affected the formation of Terkhiin Tsagaan Lake. Visit the lake shores and trek to the volcano's crater rim for a panoramic view of the surrounding terrain. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 8 — Kharkhorin: Ancient Capital and Erdene Zuu Monastery
Drive toward Kharkhorin, located within the Orkhon Valley Cultural Landscape—a region where the history of Mongolia and the larger world took shape. Kharkhorin served as the capital of the Mongol Empire; the Kharkhorin Museum houses artifacts tracing origins to the Mongol dynasties and periods preceding them. The primary site visited is Erdene Zuu Monastery, the oldest Buddhist monastery in Mongolia, founded in the late 16th century. For centuries, thousands of monks inhabited this complex and shaped Mongolian cultural and artistic development. Political purges in the 1930s diminished its collections, but the monastic grounds were preserved. Both original temples and currently active temples remain accessible for visitation. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 9 — Ongi Monastery Ruins and Trek
Drive to the ruins of Ongi Monastery in Middle Gobi province, approximately 270 kilometers southeast. The monastery once stood on both banks of the Ongi River, from which it took its name. It ranks among the three major monastic centers in Mongolian history; at its peak, over 2,000 monks lived within its walls and shaped modern Mongolian art and culture. After lunch at the camp, trek the monastic grounds—currently undergoing gradual restoration—while learning its historical significance. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 10 — Bayanzag (Flaming Cliffs): Paleontology and Silk Road History
Drive approximately 190 kilometers to Bayanzag, known as the Flaming Cliffs for the fiery colors the rock face displays at sunset. The site holds significance both paleontologically and historically: it lies on the ancient Silk Road trade route and is where the world's first fossilized dinosaur eggs were discovered. After checking into camp and lunch, visit the local information center to learn about Roy Chapman Andrews's expeditions to the region—expeditions that inspired the character of Indiana Jones. The afternoon offers extensive trekking and photography opportunities across the Flaming Cliffs. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 11 — Khongor Sand Dunes: Singing Sand and Camel Trek
Drive approximately 170 kilometers to reach the Khongor Sand Dunes camp. After lunch and rest, visit a local nomadic family in the late afternoon and ride their camels to the dunes. The dunes are known locally as Singing Sand due to the distinctive sounds the sands produce during strong winds and avalanches. The dunes extend 120 kilometers in length and 6–12 kilometers in width. Trekking to the dune tops provides expansive views of the surrounding landscape. The Khongor River flows nearby, its water supporting local greenery and life. Overnight in a standard ger camp (upgrade available).

Day 12 — Yol Valley and Gurvan Saikhan National Park: Vultures and Wildlife
Travel approximately 220 kilometers toward Gurvan Saikhan National Park. Check into camp and have lunch, then depart for Yol Valley, nicknamed Vulture Valley for the bearded vultures that nest on the tall cliffs rising above 2,000 meters. The valley lies within Gurvan Saikhan National Park, home to Argali wild sheep, Ibex, snow leopards, and falcons; sightings depend on timing and luck. Yol Valley is also known for ice glaciers that form in winter and typically melt by early July. Trek through the valley with ample photography opportunities. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 13 — Tsagaan Suvarga (White Stupa): Colored Cliffs and Photography
Depart toward Middle Gobi to visit Tsagaan Suvarga—literally meaning White Stupa—named for the appearance of the local cliffs from a distance. Stop briefly in Mandalgobi for lunch. Upon arrival, check into the local camp and enjoy a relaxed afternoon. The cliffs can be visited in the late afternoon and again the following morning. The local soil composition creates varied natural colors across the rock face, making the site a notable destination for photography. Overnight in a standard ger camp.

Day 14 — Baga Gazarin Chuluu: Granite Formations and Monastery Ruins
Depart toward Baga Gazarin Chuluu, a plateau characterized by exotic granite rock formations. After checking into the local ger camp and lunch, visit the ruins of an ancient monastery destroyed during the political purges of 1937. Walk among the rock formations themselves; the area offers trekking opportunities across distinctive terrain. Overnight in a standard ger camp.
